lines.text: What do they tell us? They form part of the seven letters
addressed to the seven Christian Churches in Asia Minor in
a time of persecution, and they are to be heard by the whole
Church. In ever fresh variations they repeat the summons:
"I come, I stand at the door!" It is a rousing, soul-stirring
summons, and its meaning may be summarized as: "This
world is not the sole or ultimate reality."
This our world has its hidden background which we are
accustomed to forget. And from that hidden beyond, there
can and there will one day break forth into this world a
power for judgment or salvation, according to the quality
of our preparedness and vigilance. We are not, as we fondly
suppose, in sole control of this world but the world and all
our activities within it will be brought to account by its
Creator and Lord. Remember what confronts all men with
imminent judgment! This our world, so familiar and homely
as we think, is not after all our true home: we shall be torn
from it and it will sink into nothingness for us on the day
when we must die. Be mindful of your last day! Our life
which we suppose to be our own does not lie within our
disposal, has not the unequivocal goal which we assume for
it, nor the completeness of meaning which we would like
to lend it. A higher hand governs its affairs, unseen, and
may at any moment intrude with a painful thrust. Be mindful
of the truth that you do not belong to yourselves!
I
"Behold, I stand at the door and knock." Who is this
"I" who stands at the door and knocks? It is eternity!
In what state will it find us?
The first warning message is very singular: "I know your
works; you are neither cold nor hot. Would that you were
cold or hot! So, because you are lukewarm, and neither
cold nor hot, I will spew you out of my mouth."
Who is being addressed here? Who is being aimed at?
The undecided man! Is indecision then the worst thing of all?
